content: The Fallopian tubes, also referred to as oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges (singular: salpinx), are two delicate tubular structures that connect the ovaries to the uterus in female mammals. These tubes are essential for the transport of ova from the ovaries to the uterus. Anatomically, there are two Fallopian tubes, each attached to one side of the uterine cornua (the upper corners of the uterus). Each tube terminates near an ovary, forming a structure called the fimbria. Importantly, the Fallopian tubes are not directly attached to the ovaries. Instead, they open into the peritoneal cavity, which is the internal space of the abdomen. This anatomical arrangement creates a direct communication pathway between the peritoneal cavity and the external environment via the vagina. In humans, the Fallopian tubes are approximately 7 to 14 cm in length. The Fallopian tube is divided into four distinct regions, progressing from the ovary to the uterus: 1. Infundibulum: This region contains the fimbriae, which help capture the ovum released from the ovary. 2. Ampulla: This is the widest section of the tube and is the most common site of fertilization. 3. Isthmus: A narrower segment that connects the ampulla to the uterus. 4. Intramural portion: This segment passes through the uterine wall and opens into the uterine cavity. Histologically, the Fallopian tube is composed of three layers: 1. Mucosa: The innermost layer, characterized by distinctive folds. These folds contain ciliated cells, which help propel the ovum, and peg cells, which secrete nutrients. The complexity of the mucosal folds varies by region, being most elaborate in the ampulla and nearly absent in the intramural portion. 2. Muscularis externa: A middle layer of smooth muscle that aids in the movement of the ovum. 3. Serosa: The outermost layer, which is a protective covering. The Fallopian tubes are highly mobile structures. Time-lapse videography has shown that they move dynamically within the pelvis. Contrary to static anatomical illustrations, the tubes do not remain fixed in position throughout the menstrual cycle. They may cross over to the opposite side or rest on top of the uterus. During ovulation, an ovum develops within an ovarian follicle. When the ovum matures, the follicle and the ovarian wall rupture, releasing the ovum into the peritoneal cavity. The fimbriae of the Fallopian tube guide the ovum into the tube, where it begins its journey toward the uterus. This movement is facilitated by the coordinated action of cilia lining the tube. The transit of the ovum through the tube can take several hours to days. If fertilization occurs within the Fallopian tube, the resulting zygote typically implants in the uterine endometrium, marking the onset of pregnancy. However, in some cases, the embryo implants within the Fallopian tube itself, leading to an ectopic pregnancy, commonly referred to as a tubal pregnancy. Embryologically, the Fallopian tubes develop from the Müllerian ducts, which are one of two pairs of embryonic ducts present in both sexes. In females, the Müllerian ducts give rise to the Fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper portion of the vagina, while the Wolffian ducts regress. In males, the Wolffian ducts develop into structures such as the epididymis and vas deferens, while the Müllerian ducts regress. The Fallopian tubes are not homologous to the vas deferens or any other male reproductive structure. Pathologically, the Fallopian tubes can be affected by pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which may lead to obstruction of the tubes. This can result in infertility or an increased risk of ectopic pregnancy. Surgically, the removal of a Fallopian tube is termed a salpingectomy. If both tubes are removed, the procedure is called a bilateral salpingectomy. When a Fallopian tube is removed along with at least one ovary, the procedure is referred to as a salpingo-oophorectomy. In cases of tubal obstruction, a surgical procedure known as tuboplasty may be performed to restore patency. The Fallopian tubes are named after Gabriele Falloppio, a 16th-century Italian anatomist who first described them. While the term Fallopian tube is eponymous, some texts use a lowercase f to reflect its integration into modern English as a standard anatomical term. The Greek word salpinx (σάλπιγξ), meaning trumpet, is also used to describe these structures due to their shape.
